h: Prosecuting dissent: politics that turns courts into a wrestling ring
dek: Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd and Srikanth Chintala say the dozens of criminal cases against Rahul Gandhi are not one leader's trouble but evidence of a method that turns dissent into a crime.
by: Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd and Srikanth Chintala
body: Rahul Gandhi, Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, has listed about 19 pending criminal cases in his election affidavits and statements, and has himself said that as many as 45 FIRs have been filed against him across the country. For Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd and lawyer Srikanth Chintala, this is proof of a method of making dissent a crime.

According to the writers, most of the cases were filed between 2014 and 2026, and almost all relate to election speeches or to things he said for people's rights as Leader of the Opposition. They fall under three heads: defamation, hurting religious feelings and spreading enmity between communities. The writers recall that Vajpayee and Sushma Swaraj attacked Nehru and Sonia Gandhi far more sharply, but were not made criminals. Even during the Emergency, opponents were political prisoners, not criminals.

The Surat case is the pivot of their argument. On the complaint of a person who was not even the subject of the remark, a lower court convicted him, he lost his seat in Parliament, and later the Supreme Court stayed the conviction. In another case, an MP-MLA court in Uttar Pradesh acquitted him on the very ground that the complainant had no right to bring the case at all.

The writers point to the test set by the Supreme Court in 2007: a crime cannot be built by pulling a few sharp words out of a whole speech, and words must be judged through the eyes of a sensible, strong-minded ordinary citizen. How, then, do so many cases survive?

Their demand is that defamation be taken out of criminal law and made a civil matter. If courts become the arena for political battles, public debate will happen in the shadow of fear and trust in the judiciary will fall. And if the Leader of the Opposition is pushed aside through court cases, a basic pillar of democracy will weaken.
nazar: On Constitution Day, this article is a reminder that the freedom of Article 19 can be taken away not only by bans but also by exhausting lawsuits. Here the punishment is not in the verdict but in the process: hearing dates, travel, lawyers' fees.

If the country's biggest opposition leader can be made to run around dozens of courts, it is not hard to guess what happens to a journalist, a student or an Adivasi (indigenous) activist. The demand to make defamation a civil matter belongs not to one party but to every citizen.
sawal: How can someone be convicted on the complaint of a person who was never mentioned?
ref: Criminal defamation
Section 500 of the old IPC (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) provides jail for defamation. In many democracies it is only a civil matter of damages.
Manzar Sayeed Khan judgment (2007)
The Supreme Court said that in a charge of inflammatory speech, the full text must be read. Words must be judged by the standard of an ordinary sensible and firm citizen, not a weak-hearted one.
ank: Criminal cases pending against Rahul Gandhi

h: Kurian Joseph committee dissolved: an unfinished record of state autonomy
dek: R. Vanchinathan, a research officer on the committee, explains that the study of Centre-state relations that the Tamil Nadu government halted midway is a loss for states across the country.
body: The Justice Kurian Joseph committee, which was examining Centre-state relations in Tamil Nadu, was dissolved on the evening of 6 November. R. Vanchinathan, who was a research officer on the committee, explains what has actually been stopped.

The committee was set up in April 2025 by the then DMK government. It was to look at which subjects moved to the Concurrent List could return to the states, and how much autonomy states should get without compromising the country's unity. According to the writer, after the Rajamannar committee of 1971, it was the first body to ask directly what should change in the Constitution; the Sarkaria and Punchhi commissions avoided touching the structure.

The first part, submitted on 16 February, had ten chapters and about a hundred recommendations: approval of two-thirds of the states for amendments affecting states, a bar on breaking up a state or lowering its status without its consent, appointment of the Governor from a list approved by the Assembly, and time limits on bills. If the freeze on delimitation is lifted, Tamil Nadu's Lok Sabha seats will fall from 39 to 29, while Bihar's will rise from 40 to 50.

The second part, covering subjects such as emergency provisions, President's Rule, the CBI and NIA, river water, minerals and forests, was about 60 percent ready. The dissolution order cites overlap with the State Law Commission. The writer's reply is that one clause of routine legal review cannot replace a dedicated study of the whole Constitution, and the order does not even say who will finish the remaining work, or when.

Drawing on the ideas of Tom Ginsburg and Aziz Huq, Vanchinathan says that people can reverse an open shock like the Emergency, but a slow decline through constitutional routes is harder to catch. Until now this decline came from the Centre; according to the writer, on 6 November it found support from a state government as well.
nazar: The federalism debate is often seen in the frame of Delhi versus the states. This story shows that a state's own government can also leave unfinished work that served its citizens, and without giving any clear reason.
Delimitation and the next Finance Commission lie ahead. The southern and other states needed solid, research-based arguments; the first part is public, and the second should be published too.
sawal: How will one clause of the Law Commission's work examine the whole Constitution?
ref: Rajamannar committee
A committee set up in 1969 by the Karunanidhi government of Tamil Nadu, whose 1971 report argued for more powers for the states. The Centre rejected it.
Freeze on delimitation
The state-wise division of Lok Sabha seats rests on the 1971 census. If the freeze is lifted, southern states that reduced their population could lose seats.

h: Gokul milk union: farmers chose the majority, the government chose the chairman
dek: Nikhil Sanjay-Rekha Adsule explains how the Maharashtra government overturned a cooperative election result with an ordinance, and why this makes a mockery of grassroots democracy.
body: The Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union, known to people as Gokul, is linked to 4.4 lakh milk producers, and its turnover in 2024-25 was about 4,000 crore rupees. Representatives of village societies elect the directors, and the directors elect the chairman. On 19 October, the panel of Congress MLC Satej Patil won 13 of the 25 seats, while the ruling Mahayuti got 12.

Nikhil Sanjay-Rekha Adsule, a researcher at IIT Delhi, explains that a quorum of 14 directors was needed to elect the chairman. On 29 October, the 12 Mahayuti directors stayed away and the meeting was put off. The straightforward course was to call a second meeting. Instead, on 4 November the state cabinet approved a change to the cooperative law, and on 6 November the Governor issued an ordinance.

The ordinance lets the government nominate five people to the boards of unions with a turnover above 500 crore rupees that receive government aid, and four of them can also vote in the chairman's election. According to the writer, this reverses the state's 2013 provision, which came after the 97th constitutional amendment and barred co-opted members from voting in the election of office-bearers.

On 10 November, on the direction of the Bombay High Court, two ballot boxes were kept, one for the elected directors and the other for the government nominees. Rajesh Patil of the Ajit Pawar faction won by 16 votes to 13: 12 votes from his own directors and four from the government's people. The court did not stay the ordinance, but tied the result to the outcome of the pending petitions.

The writer cites Germany's 1976 co-determination law, under which workers and shareholders have equal shares on the board and the government does not jump in on the plea of public interest. His suggestion is that government nominees should check the accounts and make their objections public, but the right to elect the chairman should stay with the producers' elected representatives.
nazar: Cooperatives have been the first school of village democracy, especially in Maharashtra, where milk and sugar societies gave farmers bargaining power. If the law is changed the moment a majority is lost, the farmer will learn that an ordinance is a bigger power than the vote.
Today this formula has been tried on a milk union; tomorrow the same logic could reach panchayats and municipal bodies.
sawal: On a board where farmers gave a majority, how did the government win?
ref: 97th constitutional amendment
The 2011 amendment that recognised forming a cooperative society as a fundamental right and added Part IX-B to the Constitution. It speaks of democratic management of societies and timely elections.
Co-determination law, Germany
A 1976 German law under which half the seats on the supervisory boards of large companies belong to employees' representatives.

h: On Constitution Day, fear alongside reverence
dek: Rajendra Chandrakant Rai starts from the history of the Constituent Assembly and comes to Election Commission appointments, saying that this 26 November demands an account of the wounds dealt to the Constitution.
body: 26 November is the day of the Constitution that made India a democratic republic and gave every adult citizen the right to vote. Rajendra Chandrakant Rai recalls that Tilak raised the demand for a Constituent Assembly in 1895, and that after Partition the Assembly shrank from 389 to 299 members, including 15 women, 26 Scheduled Caste members and 33 Scheduled Tribe members.

But the writer says that this time, faith in the Constitution is mixed with fear, because the government's treatment of constitutional institutions is under question. His first example is the Election Commission, set up as an autonomous body under Article 324 on 25 January 1950, whose head can be removed only by impeachment.

The 2023 law removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and made it a committee of the Prime Minister, the Home Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, in which the government's majority is assured. According to the writer, Gyanesh Kumar was appointed at midnight despite Rahul Gandhi's objection, and while the matter was pending in the Supreme Court. He also repeats the allegations of crores of names being cut from voter lists and of questions raised about EVMs.

Rai cites Freedom House's 2021 report and V-Dem's assessment, which lowered India's freedom rating and described it as sliding towards electoral autocracy. Drawing on the book by Levitsky and Ziblatt, he says that democracies today do not die in a single blast; elections go on and every step looks small.

According to the writer, this is what is happening in India: fundamental rights and the Directive Principles are being made meaningless, there are allegations of spying through Pegasus, and minorities are being pushed out of their standing as citizens. For him, this Constitution Day is an account of the wounds of the past years.
nazar: Constitution Day has now become a day of both government celebrations and opposition protests. The strength of this article is that it links the history of the Constituent Assembly directly to today's Election Commission: the institution that was given the strongest protection now has its head chosen in the government's fist.

For voters whose names were cut from the lists, the Constitution's first promise, one person one vote, is itself at stake. Defending the Constitution today means, first of all, bringing those names back.
sawal: Who chooses the head of a Commission shielded by impeachment?
ref: Chief Election Commissioner law, 2023

In the Anoop Baranwal case (2023), the Supreme Court had said the Chief Justice should be on the selection committee. In the new law, Parliament replaced him with a Union minister chosen by the Prime Minister.
V-Dem
A research institute at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden that measures democracies around the world. Since 2021 it has placed India in the category of electoral autocracy.

h: Is the international court ready to bow to Trump's threat?
dek: In Al Jazeera, Mark Kersten warns that member states are talking of changing the Rome Statute to escape US sanctions, and the biggest gainers would be Netanyahu, Putin and Myanmar's generals.
body: Legal expert Mark Kersten says preparations are under way to hollow out the International Criminal Court (ICC) from within, and the job could be done by its own member states. The Trump administration has given six months' grace before imposing harsh sanctions on the court, so that member states can find a 'solution'. The host country, the Netherlands, has admitted that it is talking to the US.

The US demands that the court should never be able to try citizens of countries that are not ICC members, wherever the crime took place. According to Amnesty chief Agnès Callamard, it is also demanding immunity for heads of state and the closure of the Palestine investigation. The writer points out that Americans faced no real threat: the court's judges recently closed the investigation into US crimes in Afghanistan themselves.

According to the writer, the real gain goes first to Netanyahu, who faces charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity over the Gaza war. Israel is not a member, but Palestine is, which is why the court could take up this case. Trump himself has said the sanctions are for Netanyahu. The warrant issued against Putin over the abduction of Ukrainian children would also become ineffective.

The third name is Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing. The International Court of Justice recently ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, and the ICC prosecutor sought a warrant for him in 2024. This case was built through member state Bangladesh, where the Rohingya were pushed.

The writer argues that in a world where no one has to answer, violence becomes not the exception but the norm. Of the 125 member states, none has yet said clearly that there will be no bargain over the Rome Statute. Washington cannot break the court alone, so the decision is in the hands of the member states.
nazar: India is not a member of the ICC, but it is not apart from this fight. Right in our neighbourhood, Bangladesh has opened a path to justice for the Rohingya, and Rohingya refugees living in India also fled the same genocide. If powerful countries begin deciding whom the law applies to, the weakest peoples will be the first left without support.
Countries of the Global South have often complained that this court acts only against African leaders. Now that it has reached powerful people, saving it is a test for these very countries.
sawal: Will the Gaza warrants become the price of six months' grace?
ref: Rome Statute
The 1998 treaty that created the International Criminal Court. It gives the right to try individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The difference between the ICC and the ICJ
The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague tries individuals. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the UN court that settles disputes between countries.

h: A referendum on new provinces: where will it take Pakistan?
dek: In Dawn, Zahid Hussain writes that the 'administrative reset' plan being shaped outside Parliament is inflaming Sindh and could become a tool to concentrate power further.
body: Pakistan's government appears to be moving towards a referendum on creating new provinces. The minister for parliamentary affairs has said it will certainly happen, and according to the defence minister the process could move forward early next year. Journalist and author Zahid Hussain asks where this road actually leads.

The sharpest opposition is from Sindh. PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari has warned that a forced division of provinces, especially of Sindh, could lead to bloodshed. The writer also sees an irony here: Bilawal now speaks of the supremacy of Parliament and restoring trust in the judiciary, while his own party helped pass the 26th and 27th amendments, which reined in the independence of the courts.

According to the writer, this whole debate is taking place outside Parliament. The idea of a 'reset' was floated by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose ties to the establishment are well known. The Prime Minister and the PML-N are silent, coalition partners are fighting among themselves, and to this day no concrete plan, not even the referendum question, has been put before the cabinet. The writer calls the government a boat without a rudder.

Many questions remain unanswered. Will there be one question for the whole country or a separate one for each province? When Sindh's elected Assembly has already rejected such a proposal, how will this vote be applied there? The writer favours decentralisation and strong local governments, but says that creating provinces through a referendum, bypassing the constitutional process, could be fatal for national unity.

All this is happening at a time when Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan are struggling with violent militancy and the economy is shaky. The writer's final warning is that a desired result can be extracted from a referendum, and such a gamble on so important a constitutional question could bring down the whole system.
nazar: This debate next door reminds us of our own. When the borders of provinces, the federal structure or basic questions of the Constitution are decided from above, bypassing elected assemblies, that is not democracy but the centralisation of power. The splitting of Jammu and Kashmir into two also happened without an assembly.
For ordinary people in Pakistan, especially Sindhis and Baloch, the real question is the one the writer raises: will the decision be made in Parliament or somewhere else?
sawal: How will any vote overturn the 'no' of Sindh's elected Assembly?
ref: 26th and 27th amendments
Recent amendments to Pakistan's constitution which critics accuse of reducing the independence of the judiciary and strengthening the hand of the establishment.
PPP
The Pakistan Peoples Party, the Bhutto family's party, whose strongest base is Sindh. It is a key partner in the power arrangement formed after the disputed 2024 election.

h: Spain's lesson: lofty words, empty homes, and the right at the door
dek: In openDemocracy, British Labour MP Jon Trickett writes that the Sánchez government's half-hearted policies turned the rent crisis into a fire, and that this is a warning for every centre-left party.
body: In the view of British Labour MP Jon Trickett, Spain today is the clearest example of a politics in which the language is progressive and the work follows the old pattern. Amid spreading movements over the housing crisis, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election, and polls show the right-wing Popular Party in the lead, with possible support from the far-right Vox.

The writer does not deny Sánchez's good work. In power since 2018, his government curbed precarious temporary contracts, encouraged permanent jobs and raised the minimum wage. But workers are still being crushed, because house prices rose 70-80 percent between 2015 and 2025, and low earners spend 40 to 60 percent of their income on rent. For the writer, this is rentier capitalism, which swallows every gain.

The face of this crisis became 87-year-old Maricarmen. This wheelchair-using pensioner had been a tenant in a Madrid flat for seven decades. A corporate landlord bought the building and wanted to raise the rent. The courts had stopped her eviction three times, but in September the police carried her out on a stretcher, giving her half an hour to pack her things. She died in hospital. After this, tents went up in several cities, including at Madrid's Puerta del Sol.

Tenant unions are now demanding that rents be halved, that empty speculative homes be seized and that tourist apartments be banned, and there is talk of a general strike. The writer sees the same pattern on Gaza: criticism of Israel abroad, while defence supplies continued for months at home.

The writer concludes that such 'orphan words', with no structural change behind them, fill people with despair and open the way for the far right. He argues for public housing on a large scale, strict rent control and public ownership of essential services.
nazar: Tenants in Mumbai, Bengaluru or Delhi will recognise this story: rent rising faster than salaries, builders' flats lying empty, and bulldozers running over settlements. We do not even have the strength of tenant unions here, and government housing schemes are mostly limited to loan subsidies.
Spain shows that when centrist parties are afraid of a basic question like housing, the anger does not go away; the right puts it in its own account.
sawal: Maricarmen got half an hour; how many years to change the policy?
ref: Vox
Spain's far-right party, founded in 2013, which rose quickly on anti-migrant and nationalist slogans.
Puerta del Sol
Madrid's central square. In 2011 the tents of the 'Indignados' movement were pitched here, and it is a symbol of Spain's big mass movements.

h: A flood of Form 6 in UP: over four lakh applications in one day
dek: According to an Alt News analysis, applications to add names jumped from two thousand a day after the draft roll came out to 4.16 lakh on 22 November.
body: After the SIR, Uttar Pradesh is now going through a Special Summary Revision, and applications on Form 6, used to add names, have suddenly surged. The Wire has republished this investigation by Alt News. In the first fortnight, an average of ten thousand applications came in each day. After the draft roll was published on 17 November, they reached 31 thousand, then 68 thousand, 2.31 lakh on 21 November and 4.16 lakh on 22 November. On 22 November alone, more forms were filled than in the first twenty days of November.

The report places this surge in a political context. On 30 October, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath told a BJP meeting that more than 1.25 crore Hindu voters were missing from the roll, and according to reports the party set a target of adding ten to twenty-five thousand names in every seat. On 22 November, 191 of the 403 seats received more than a thousand applications, while before 17 November no seat had received that many.

Matching against the 2.89 crore names cut in the SIR showed that of about 10.4 lakh applications checked, only 45 thousand were from people whose names had been cut. Duplication was found too: 10,773 people filled the form more than once, 427 from two different seats, and in Meerut's Siwalkhas seat, 44 applications gave the same address.

In contrast, in many seats of western districts such as Bijnor, Muzaffarnagar, Saharanpur, Rampur and Shamli, almost no applications came in during these days, while Kheri, Ghaziabad and Agra were at the top.
nazar: Very few of the crores of names cut in the SIR are coming back, but the wave of new names rose in the very days the ruling party handed out targets. The voter roll cannot be the ledger of a party's booth campaign. The Election Commission should explain how duplicate applications and those with the same address are being checked, and where the cut voters are in the districts from which applications are missing.
sawal: In seats where not a single form came in, where did the voters go?
ref: Form 6
The application to add a new name to the voter roll or to move a name from one constituency to another.
Special Summary Revision
The regular correction of the voter roll. In UP its draft roll was published on 17 November, and the final roll is due in January 2027.

h: Notice five hours before the flight, Saurav Das stopped at the airport
dek: The co-convener of the Cockroach Janata Party was stopped from going to London after being handed a notice about the birthplace in his passport; he has approached the Delhi High Court.
body: Saurav Das, co-convener of the Cockroach Janata Party, was turned back from the immigration counter at Delhi airport on the night of 23 November. He was to go to London to speak at the Oxford Union and attend events at universities such as the LSE, Cambridge and Edinburgh. The flight was at one in the morning, and a show-cause notice from the Chennai regional passport office arrived by email at half past seven that same evening.

The notice seeks an explanation about the birthplace written in his 2019 passport application, alleges concealment of facts and warns that the passport will be impounded if he does not reply within seven days. A government official told the paper that the date of birth, birthplace and father's name do not match across his passport and Aadhaar papers. The External Affairs Ministry spokesperson said on Wednesday that such notices are issued when law enforcement agencies report irregularities.

Das says he has no problem replying, but sending a notice a few hours before a flight is unjust. He has travelled abroad twice since 2019 and links this inquiry to his politics. The notice came after a businessman's public interest petition in the Madras High Court seeking an inquiry into his citizenship.
On Wednesday, Das filed a plea in the Delhi High Court, which was listed for hearing on 26 November. In October, he was also arrested ahead of a protest at Jantar Mantar.
nazar: The timing of the notice is itself a statement. If there really was an irregularity in the papers, why did nobody see it in seven years, and why was it seen just before he was to speak abroad? Using the passport as a tool to stop the movement of dissenters is a direct blow to the right to travel abroad given under Article 21 of the Constitution.
sawal: Why was a seven-year-old irregularity found on the very evening of the flight?
ref: Section 10(3)(b) of the Passports Act
The provision that gives the power to impound or revoke a passport obtained by concealing facts or giving wrong information.

h: Sanitation workers live 11 years less than others
dek: A new study has produced a figure that sanitation workers from Bhilai to Chennai live out in their daily lives.
body: According to a report by Reckitt and the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), the average life expectancy of sanitation workers in India is 63.8 years, which is 11.4 years less than in professional and managerial jobs and 9.6 years less than farm labourers with similar education and income. About 30 percent of their deaths are linked to toxic gases and poisoning, and only one percent have any health insurance contribution. Urban male sanitation workers had the lowest life expectancy, 62.3 years.

The Mooknayak spoke to workers in several states. In Bhilai, Bharti Pakhale has worked for eight years on eight thousand rupees a month, from six in the morning to two in the afternoon, with neither ESI nor PF, and pays for treatment out of her own pocket. In Jodhpur, contract workers get seven thousand, while permanent workers get fifty-five thousand. In Damoh, salaries arrive three months late, and were not paid even at Diwali.

In Chandigarh, a day's wage is cut when a worker falls sick. In Chennai, workers fought for months against the work being handed to a private company, went into the Cooum river in January, and won a promise of wages directly from the corporation, but permanent jobs are still pending. In Bhopal, about thirteen thousand daily-wage workers have been on strike since 3 November, demanding 25 thousand rupees a month.

According to one organisation's count, 66 sanitation workers died between February and July 2026. The workers' demands are basic: fair wages, an end to contract work, safety equipment and a national policy.
nazar: Eleven years less of life is nothing natural; it is the toll of contract work, toxic sewers and a caste-bound occupation. Those who keep cities liveable have neither insurance nor leave. Crores are spent on cleanliness campaigns, but the budget for the lives of the hands that run those campaigns is still eight thousand rupees.
sawal: On a salary of eight thousand, who will insure them against toxic gas?
ref: ESI and PF
Employees' State Insurance (money for treatment and sick leave) and the Provident Fund (savings for old age), which regular employees get.

h: Nagpur people's court puts campus casteism on trial
dek: Families of Payal Tadvi, Sahil Wakode and other students gave testimony and demanded a separate law against institutional casteism.
body: The All India Independent Scheduled Caste Association (AIISCA) held a Janata Adalat (people's court) in Nagpur on 22 November against institutional casteism and deaths. It brought together families of students who lost their lives in educational institutions, along with academics, Ambedkarite activists, lawyers and students.

Dr Payal Tadvi's mother said her daughter faced discrimination from her first day of admission at Mumbai's Nair Hospital, and that the family has been fighting for justice for seven and a half years, with obstacles put in the way deliberately. She repeated the demand for a Rohith Act. Sahil Wakode's father said that at IIT Bombay his son allegedly had to endure casteist remarks and threats, and that the family had at first advised him to bear it. His mother said that if a law had been made after Payal's death, Sahil could have been saved. Raghavi's father said four years of legal battle had broken his faith in the system.

Professor Sukhadeo Thorat said discrimination on campus is structural, and that a law alone does not change society; it needs change in education and thinking as well. The organisation's founder, Dr Rahul Sonpimple, asked why students' suffering often comes to light only after their death.
The court demanded a separate legal framework, strict enforcement of anti-discrimination rules, an independent complaints mechanism and accountability of institutions.
nazar: From Rohith Vemula to Payal Tadvi and Sahil Wakode, after every death institutions set up an inquiry committee and fall silent. When courts and commissions take years, it is a necessity for grieving families to hold their own people's court. The demand for a Rohith Act no longer belongs to one organisation, but to every parent who sent a son or daughter to study and got back a dead body.
sawal: Whom should a society that advised Sahil to bear it apologise to?
ref: Rohith Act
A demand raised after the death of Hyderabad University research scholar Rohith Vemula in 2016: a separate law to stop caste discrimination in educational institutions.
Payal Tadvi
An Adivasi (indigenous) doctor who died in Mumbai in May 2019. Three senior doctors are accused of caste harassment.

h: Supreme Court strikes down two UP laws that denied pensions
dek: Laws that barred counting daily-wage and work-charged service before regularisation towards pensions have been held unconstitutional.
body: The Supreme Court has declared two Uttar Pradesh laws unconstitutional: the 2021 law on qualifying service for pension and validation, and the 2025 law on eligibility for pension and validation. The verdict of the bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Satish Chandra Sharma came on 18 November. The case was brought by the employees' union of the groundwater department.

The background is the 2019 Prem Singh judgment, in which the court said that years of work-charged service would count towards pension. After this, the state government brought these laws and applied them retrospectively from 1961, so that years of daily-wage, temporary and muster roll work could be kept out of pensions.

The court said that once an employee is regularised, the old defect in the appointment ends, and the employer cannot later revive it, even through a retrospective law, to take away retirement rights. This violates the rights to equality and life (Articles 14, 16 and 21). Merely renaming the excluded class does not make discrimination legitimate.

Retired employees can now file their claims, which must be decided within six months. Delay will attract nine percent annual interest. On the contempt petitions, the court gave the state a final six months to pay and warned that further neglect would be treated as serious contempt.
nazar: A government twice made laws to escape a court verdict and pushed the date back sixty years, so that it would not have to pay pensions to employees who toiled for years on daily wages. The court has said plainly that injustice cannot be saved by changing names. Now we must see whether, within six months, money reaches elderly employees, or contempt petitions again.
sawal: Whose idea was it to go back to 1961 to take away pensions?
ref: Work-charged employees
Employees hired for a particular construction or project, whose wages come from that work's budget and who are not on regular posts.
Prem Singh judgment (2019)
The Supreme Court ruling that work-charged service before regularisation will count towards pension.

h: Book on Basavanna: FIR against the author, copies seized
dek: US-based author Ravi Hanjagimutt has petitioned the Karnataka High Court to quash the case filed over 'Basava Mantapa'.
body: Ravi Hanjagimutt, author of 'Basava Mantapa', a Kannada book on the twelfth-century social reformer Basavanna, has approached the Karnataka High Court to quash the FIR filed against him. The book was released in Bengaluru on 15 November and contains his columns published in the newspaper 'Vishwavani', which use sources such as the Mysore Gazetteer and the Basava Purana to examine the origins of the Veerashaiva-Lingayat faith.

On the complaint of Basava Samiti president Arvind Jatti, a case was registered on 19 November at Bengaluru's High Grounds police station under several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The allegation is that in a TV interview the author called Basavanna a thief and a murderer and made objectionable remarks about the Lingayat community. The same day, the state cabinet approved seizing the book, and on 22 November the Home Department issued the seizure notification, citing public order and communal harmony.

In the petition, the author says that in the interview he only set out his historical sources and the traditional interpretation of some vachanas (devotional verses), with no intention of insulting anyone. According to him, on 21 November he was stopped at Kochi airport on the basis of a lookout circular, taken into police custody and given a notice. He describes the complaint as enmity arising from his earlier writing on the misuse of government property given to the Basava Samiti.
nazar: The answer to disagreement with an interpretation of history is another book, not an FIR and seizure. Basavanna himself was a symbol of the tradition of questioning. The Congress government too is taking, in the name of faith, the same path it complains about in BJP governments: guarding a book before it can be read.
sawal: Why fear a book on Basavanna, who asked questions?
ref: Basavanna
A twelfth-century Kannada social reformer and composer of vachanas, who spoke out against caste and ritualism. The Lingayat tradition regards him as its founder.
BNSS Section 98
The power of the government to declare forfeited a book or publication it considers to be inciting enmity between communities.

h: Students on sit-in at Kolkata's SRFTI allege they are being secretly filmed
dek: Students of the film institute, on a sit-in for 57 days, have accused the security in-charge of assault and of groping a woman student.
place: Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute, Kolkata
ask: Stop the surveillance, remove the security in-charge, hold an inquiry headed by a woman
body: Students who have been on a sit-in for about 57 days at the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata allege that for weeks the administration has been having them recorded on private phones without their consent. The latest incident came when a woman student on her way to the toilet in the administrative building found a security guard following her and filming her.

According to the students, when asked, the guard said he was acting on orders, but no written order was shown. When the students went to the security in-charge, Prabir Kumar Munshi, for an answer, he allegedly assaulted them and groped a woman student. One woman student's thumb was injured and another was left with swelling and bruises. The students also allege that police present on campus stood and watched, and that the Registrar and the Dean did not come even when called.

The sit-in began after the attacks of 27 September and 4 October, when students were attacked for protesting an event on campus by an organisation linked to the RSS. The students' union has demanded a written explanation from the Vice-Chancellor, preservation of all recordings and CCTV footage, Munshi's removal until an inquiry is done, and an independent inquiry headed by a woman.
nazar: An institution that could not act against the attackers is now recording even its own students' sleep. These are upside-down priorities. The right to privacy does not end at the campus gate, and the safety of women students cannot be put off in the name of discipline.
sawal: Who, in the end, gave the order to follow a student to the toilet?
ref: Internal Complaints Committee
A committee every institution must set up under the 2013 law on sexual harassment at the workplace, to look into complaints of molestation and harassment.

h: Girls from a Ratlam Adivasi hostel walk five kilometres to the Collectorate
dek: With no blankets in the biting cold and poor food, the girl students staged a sit-in at the Collectorate.
ask: Blankets for the cold, and proper food as per the menu
body: In Ratlam, Madhya Pradesh, dozens of girl students of the government Kanya Shiksha Parisar on Sagod Road walked about five kilometres to the Collectorate on Wednesday and sat down there in protest. The hostel is run by the Tribal Affairs Department.

The girls complained that even after the bitter cold had set in, they had not been given blankets. They also questioned the quality and variety of the food. They said that instead of the special dishes listed on the menu, dal-baati was served again and again. They also listed the lack of other basic facilities in the hostel.

Collector Ajay Katesaria directed officials of the Tribal Affairs Department to resolve the complaints. Assistant Commissioner Priyanka Rai and Principal Gantantra Mehta came to the Collectorate and heard the girls out. Rai promised quick action and also inspected the arrangements at the hostel.

At first the girls refused to end the sit-in. After the administration stepped in, they said they were satisfied and went back to the hostel. The report does not make clear whether blankets were handed out or the menu was changed.
nazar: Blankets and decent food are not a favour; they are the minimum duty of a government hostel. When Adivasi (indigenous) girls have to walk five kilometres just to say they are cold, the question is about the inspection system, which never reached them before they reached the Collectorate.
sawal: Why did they have to walk to the Collectorate for a blanket?
ref: Kanya Shiksha Parisar
Residential schools of Madhya Pradesh's Tribal Affairs Department, where girls from Adivasi areas live and study.

h: Women at Delhi's Vasant Udyan declare: the park is ours
dek: On the international day against violence on women, women of all ages gathered in a South Delhi park and demanded an equal right to public spaces.
ask: Streets, parks and footpaths should be safe and open to women
body: On the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, women of different ages gathered at Vasant Udyan in South Delhi on Wednesday. The gathering, called 'Hain Haq Hamara Hissedari' (Our right, our share), was organised by the Centre for Equity and Inclusion (CEQUIN) and the Hissedari Partners Collective as part of the global 16-day campaign against gender violence. Placards in the park read 'The park is ours' and 'Clothes have no gender'.

CEQUIN co-founder Lora K. Prabhu said the laws are piecemeal and the problem is not looked at as a whole. On the closing of Aastha Kunj park after a report of sexual violence against a minor, she said that removing women from public spaces is the wrong cure.

A CEQUIN study was also released on the occasion, based on responses from 1,588 women, girls and LGBTQ people. According to it, 88.9 per cent feel afraid in their neighbourhood park after dark, and 87.5 per cent while walking to a metro or bus stop. 76.4 per cent complained of dark footpaths and 79.5 per cent of men staring, passing remarks and stalking. 80.5 per cent do not even know which department to complain to.
nazar: Shutting a park is the easiest government answer, but it does not remove the fear; it only shuts women inside their homes. The study's most important figure is that most women do not even know who is accountable. Along with lights and footpaths, the address of accountability should also be made public.
sawal: Which office should a complaint about a dark park go to?
ref: 16-day campaign
A global campaign held every year from 25 November to 10 December (Human Rights Day), which raises awareness and demands action against gender violence.

h: Deficit school teachers' sit-in goes on in Shillong over dearness allowance and pension
dek: Sitting outside the Meghalaya Board's office, the teachers summed up their fight in three demands: justice, security and dignity.
ask: Pay the pending dearness allowance and restore the old CPF 2023 scheme
body: The sit-in by teachers of Meghalaya's deficit schools continued on Tuesday, 24 November, outside the office of the Meghalaya Board of School Education (MBOSE) in Shillong. Teachers from the Mawkhar-Jaiaw and Sohra zones also joined the protest that day.

Speaking to the media, teacher Aibantiplang Rynjah listed the movement's three demands: justice, security and dignity. Justice means the pending dearness allowance (DA), which was promised before the Puja. According to him, employees of other government departments have already received 53 per cent DA, while deficit teachers are still stuck at 49 per cent, though price rise hits everyone equally.

Security is about pensions. Rynjah said the CPF 2023 scheme was better, because it kept teachers recruited before and after 1 April 2010 separate and fixed a contribution of 10 per cent of basic pay, which the government matched. The new CPF 2026 fixes neither the rate of contribution nor the categories, which has worried teachers close to retirement.

Speaking of dignity, he asked why senior, retired and deceased teachers get no respect, when many officers and professionals were taught by them. He said that once they get their due, teachers will happily go back to their classrooms.
nazar: Deficit schools are the backbone of school education in Meghalaya, yet their teachers hang between government and private. For one government to give its employees 53 per cent allowance and teachers 49 per cent is a discrimination that should have ended before any sit-in.
sawal: Same price rise, so why a four per cent gap in the allowance?
ref: Deficit school
Schools in Meghalaya run by private bodies, whose teachers' salaries are paid by the state government as a deficit grant.

h: Sacked power workers climb high-tension towers in Bhubaneswar
dek: Contract workers on a sit-in for 55 days climbed several towers in the city to demand reinstatement; three were arrested.
ask: Reinstate the sacked workers and review power privatisation
body: Contract power workers who lost their jobs in Odisha climbed several high-tension towers in and around Bhubaneswar on Wednesday, 25 November. Two to four workers climbed each tower at Acharya Vihar, Satya Vihar, Natala near the Secretariat, Hi-Tech Square, Mancheswar, CIFA and Pitapalli. Police and fire services cut power to the lines, spread nets and asked them to come down. Some stayed up for hours, demanding a firm assurance.

The workers have been on a sit-in at Lower PMG for about 55 days. Some have been on an indefinite hunger strike for more than three weeks and about 50 have ended up in hospital. Their demands are reinstatement, action on the Chief Minister's earlier assurances, minimum wages for meter readers and bill collectors, and a review of outsourcing and privatisation in the power sector.

Deputy Chief Minister K.V. Singh Deo, who holds the energy department, told the Assembly that climbing towers was unacceptable and warned of strict action. According to him, notices to 3,155 workers have been withdrawn, but the demand to reinstate 192 customer care assistants removed in October 2025 has not been accepted. Three people who climbed a 33 kV tower at Acharya Vihar were rescued and arrested, and a case was filed against them under ESMA.
nazar: When a man has to climb a 400 kV tower to be heard, it is the story not of a protest but of broken roads to dialogue. The answer to a 55-day sit-in and hunger strike should be face-to-face talks, not ESMA and arrests.
sawal: Why is the government so firm against reinstating 192 workers?
ref: ESMA
The Essential Services Maintenance Act, under which the government can ban strikes and protests in essential services such as electricity and make arrests.

h: Cauvery delta farmers bring ploughs and bullocks to remind the government of its loan waiver promise
dek: A federation of 50 farmers' groups protested in Tiruchi, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam, demanding an unconditional loan waiver and drought relief.
place: Tiruchi and the Cauvery delta districts
ask: A full crop loan waiver as promised in the election, and compensation of 40,000 per acre
body: A federation of 50 farmers' groups held protests in several districts of Tamil Nadu's Cauvery delta on Wednesday. They want the state government to announce a fresh crop loan waiver, as Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay promised during the Assembly election campaign.

The farmers say the promise was of a full waiver regardless of the loan amount, but the government later announced a waiver with conditions. Assurances from ministers achieved nothing, so they will now agitate indefinitely. Their other grievance is water: the state could not get its share of water from Karnataka, so both the kuruvai and samba crops failed. They are demanding that the whole delta be declared drought-hit and that Rs 40,000 be paid as compensation for every acre.

In Tiruchi, led by the federation's coordinator Vivekanandan, farmers gathered near the Collectorate with bullocks and ploughs. When police stopped the rally, they marched in a procession and handed a memorandum to the District Collector and the Joint Registrar of Cooperative Societies. Similar protests were held in Thanjavur, Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam.
nazar: The delta farmer is hit twice over: no water came from upstream, and the bank loan is still unpaid below. Adding conditions to an election promise afterwards is a betrayal of trust, and for the new government this is the first big test of how it keeps its biggest promise.
sawal: It was 'no conditions' during the election, so who added them later?
ref: Kuruvai and samba
The two main paddy crops of the Cauvery delta: kuruvai is the short-duration summer crop, samba the long-duration main crop.

h: Kalimantan's fires: the slow fight to farm without burning
dek: A long drought in Indonesian Borneo burned both forests and farms, and some villages are now trying a way of farming without fire.
body: The rains have returned, but the fire season is not fully over in Indonesia's Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo). According to this Mongabay report, about 684,000 hectares burned here between January and September, about 36 per cent of the land burned in the whole country, though the region is only 28 per cent of the country's land. A strong El Nino cut the rainfall and the drought stretched longer than even the bad years of 2015 and 2019. By the health ministry's count, 12.5 million people had been hit by fire or smoke by September.

Katarina Rina, a 53-year-old farmer living on the edge of the Gunung Naning protected forest in Ketapang district, says this was the first time such a big fire reached the farms in her area. Her jengkol orchard was reduced to ash. Saro Halawa, a farmer nearby, accepts that clearing land by burning is not sustainable, but says he cannot afford the cost of giving it up.

Planet Indonesia is teaching farmers to plant fruit and native trees on fallow land, so there is less need to cut new forest. In Seruyan district, a group called Gawi Bapakat has been running fire-free farming with six Dayak indigenous villages since 2024: hand tractors, seeds, and home-made organic manure in place of ash. Yadi, 66, of Tumbang Gugup, says unburned soil stays fertile and moist for longer.

But the problem is big. According to anthropologist Sofyan Ansori, such experiments run on a small scale and stall as soon as the support stops, because ordinary farmers cannot bear the cost of tractors, fuel and chemicals. A study by the local group SIAR shows that 63 per cent of this year's fires in West Kalimantan were in licensed oil palm areas, nearly half of them on peatland that had burned before.
nazar: It is easy to put all the blame for the fires on the small farmer's matchbox, but the figures show that most fires break out on company plantations and drained peatland. Farmers need alternatives, and the government has to bear the cost of those alternatives, not a few days of help from donors.
India's debate on stubble burning teaches the same lesson: until clearing a field without fire is cheap and easy, fines and sermons alone will not stop the smoke.
sawal: Who will make the companies that drain peat pay the price of the fires?
ref: Peatland
Marshy land with a thick layer of plants rotting over centuries. Once drained, it catches fire easily and the fire can smoulder for months.
El Nino
A warming of the Pacific Ocean that can cut rainfall and bring drought to South-East Asia and India.

h: Colombia at a crossroads: a picture of peace on a wall of murdered comrades
dek: This Al Jazeera Witness film follows a former FARC fighter and artist to look at a fragile peace that is still being stained with blood ten years on.
body: This documentary in Al Jazeera's 'Witness' series is by filmmaker Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi. At its centre is Yuheni Izquierdo, who once fought with the FARC guerrilla group and now paints. According to the film's introduction, she is painting a mural in memory of comrades who signed the peace agreement and were later killed.

The background is well known. In 2016, after long talks in Havana, the capital of Cuba, the Colombian government and FARC reached an agreement that formally ended an armed conflict that had lasted more than fifty years. Thousands of fighters laid down their arms and the group turned into a political party. The same year, President Juan Manuel Santos was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

But the peace on paper did not fully reach the ground. According to Al Jazeera's description, hundreds of former fighters, known in Colombia as 'peace signatories', have been killed since the agreement in revenge attacks and in fights for control of territory. In areas that FARC left, other armed groups and criminal gangs moved in.

Yuheni's fear is that the rising violence could push the country back into the era that, according to the film's introduction, took more than 450,000 lives. Her hope is that the faces painted on the wall will convince people that lasting peace is possible.

Deshkaal is not giving details here of which village or town the film was shot in, who else appears with Yuheni, or what is said at which point. This introduction is based on Al Jazeera's page and on well-known facts about Colombia's peace agreement. The rest can only be had by watching the film.
The film's title is itself a question: ten years after the agreement, which way will Colombia go, towards protecting those who gave up the gun, or back to the old cycle of violence?
nazar: A peace agreement is not a signature on one day but years of protection. A state that cannot save the lives of those who laid down arms sends the next rebellion the message that agreements cannot be trusted.

In India's own regions too, whether the North-East or the forests of central India, life after surrenders and accords needs just as serious attention. An artist's wall reminds us that giving peace a face is also politics.
sawal: If those who give up the gun are not protected, who will sign the next agreement?
ref: FARC
Colombia's left-wing guerrilla group (from 1964), which laid down arms after the 2016 agreement and formed a political party.
Havana peace agreement
The 2016 agreement between the Colombian government and FARC, reached after four years of talks in Cuba.

h: Thirty kilometres that took generations to cover
dek: Manish Chaurasia's essay ties together the Bansi river, his grandmother's unkept promise and a job at a government college in Bihar.
body: On a map, a thirty-kilometre line looks short, but the writer says covering this very distance in life can take a lifetime. For his family, Bansi was always a place out of stories, a name that came up again and again in talk at home.

The essay begins with the family's oral memory. His grandfather's wedding party went by bullock cart, and the groom refused to touch the kheer (rice pudding) until he was given a bicycle. Meanwhile his hungry father and uncle ate the kheer and told the guests that the groom was sulking inside. When the bicycle came, all three rode home on it together.

The Bansi rises in the Terai of Nepal, flows through Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and meets the Narayani, or Gandak, near Pipraghat. A local saying goes that one dip in the Bansi earns as much merit as a hundred trips to Kashi, which makes it a pilgrimage of householders and working people. In a tale told by Ramai Baba, the village storyteller, Ram's wedding party stopped here on its way back from Janakpur, and the names of nearby villages recall that halt.

In his childhood, every Kartik Purnima the village filled tractors and went to bathe in the river. Every year his grandmother would say she would take him next time, but that next time never came, and she passed away. The writer has not forgotten that ache to this day.

Then the story turns to his own life. After an interview in Patna, he got a job as an assistant professor in Bihar and was posted to Pipraghat Degree College in West Champaran, about thirty kilometres from his village in Kushinagar. Despite his hesitation over giving up three years of fellowship, he took the job, and now lives in a rented room on the banks of the Bansi.
nazar: This essay shows that in the folk memory of Purvanchal and Champaran, river, pilgrimage and livelihood are tied by a single thread. A researcher giving up a fellowship to go to a remote government college is as big a story as Ram's wedding party; it is just that nobody sings it.
sawal: To which riverbank did a grandmother's unkept promise bring her grandson?
ref: Kartik Purnima
The full moon of the month of Kartik, when north India has an old tradition of bathing in rivers and holding fairs.
Gandak (Narayani)
A river that rises in Nepal and joins the Ganga in Bihar. Small rivers like the Bansi flow into it.
photo_note: The month of Kartik, a Barahmasa painting, Jaipur

h: A son's reckoning after his father is gone
dek: Durgesh Kumar Sajal's memoir tries to understand a stern father raised in hardship, who hid his illness to save his son's education.
body: This memoir speaks directly to the father. The writer accepts that his father was a typical father of his time: strict, quick to anger, harsh of speech. Years later he understands that the fault was not his father's but that of the circumstances he grew up in.

According to the writer, his father lost his own father at fifteen, had to leave his studies unfinished, and was married at seventeen. Without a job, running a household became a burden, relatives kept their distance and he was cheated too. From this he drew the lesson that no one should marry without steady work, because the hardest blow of unemployment falls on the girl who marries into the house.

The same father was the strongest supporter of his son's education. He pushed for admission to a good institute in Bhopal, got him a separate room to prepare for the JRF and his first table and chair, and taught him dohas, chaupais and savaiyas (forms of Hindi verse) amid the scolding. When others discouraged an MA in Hindi, his father said, study what you like. In 2013 he put off getting a sore on his cheek checked, to save money.

When the son got into a PhD, his father was overjoyed, but soon fell ill and kept it hidden. Tests found cancer that had spread to both lungs. During treatment in Nagpur the doctor said there was little time left, and the writer hid the truth from his father. To the very end, his father worried about his son's career.
Three years later the writer says the world seems more selfish than before, and he has failed in two interviews, yet hope remains that his father lives on in his blood.
nazar: This is private grief, but beneath it lies a social document: unemployment, the cost of treatment, and parents staking their own health on their children's education. The same story quietly repeats itself in millions of homes across the Hindi belt.
sawal: Who paid the price of a check-up put off to save money?
ref: JRF
Junior Research Fellowship, a research grant awarded through the UGC-NET exam, on which many researchers' studies depend.
Phag
Folk songs sung in the Holi season. The writer's father wanted to write them but never found the time.

h: Viveki Rai: when nothing surprises us any more
dek: Hindwi has published a satirical essay by Viveki Rai from a 1995 book, which argues that indifference is more dangerous for a society than even hatred.
body: This essay by Viveki Rai, a writer of rural life, is taken from his book 'Jagat Tapovan So Kiyo' (He made the world a hermitage), published in 1995. It opens with the Yaksha's questions in the Mahabharata, where Yudhishthira says the greatest wonder is that even after seeing people die every day, man still wants to live. Rai says that today's Yudhishthira would say the wonder is that nothing surprises anyone any more.

He gives the example of a railway station one evening. The train came an hour late, no coach had lights, the station's power was also out, and people were groping their way in the dark. Back home it struck him that seeing all this had not surprised him in the least.

The essay lists many things that have come to be accepted as normal: no electricity at Diwali, no water at Holi, reports of women burned for dowry, new government buildings collapsing in the first rain, and, according to the writer, about 12,500 primary schools in Uttar Pradesh that ran under trees. Bribes have come to be called a convenience fee, and corruption, courtesy.

Mentioning the failure of two satellite launches from Sriharikota in 1988, Rai draws a line between shock and surprise. Surprise is the mark of a living society full of hope, while constant shocks leave people hopeless. In his view, after Independence the wings of aspiration were slowly clipped.
In the end he writes that the greatest wonder is that no one lives for the country any more. Hatred at least is a sign of attachment, but widespread indifference is suicidal for the country.
nazar: This thirty-year-old essay still feels just as fresh, and that is its biggest warning. In a society that is not shocked by broken bridges, sold exam papers and helpless hospitals, those in power no longer need to answer for anything.
sawal: What news today truly surprises us?
ref: Viveki Rai (1924-2016)
Hindi and Bhojpuri writer from Ghazipur, who portrayed changing village life in his personal essays and in novels such as 'Sonamati'.
Yaksha's questions
An episode in the Mahabharata in which a Yaksha (nature spirit) asks Yudhishthira questions about life and dharma.
photo_note: Purification by muddy water, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: A girl doing push-ups, and the gaze of those watching
dek: Through gyms, tattoos, clothes and social media, Deepti Kushwah's essay shows how today's woman is claiming her body and her choices.
body: The essay opens with a scene: a boy and a girl have to do push-ups together. The boy pulls off his T-shirt at once, and every eye turns to the girl to see if she will hesitate. Without a care she takes off her top and enters the contest in a sports bra. For the writer, the real point is not taking off clothes but the ease that does not care about the camera or what people think.

She then lists many signs of the changing image of women. Women have themselves broken or widened the old standards of beauty, of a slim waist and low weight. Women are seen in gyms doing weight training, boxing and powerlifting, and muscles are no longer something to hide. To critics who ask why, the writer's answer is simple: she will do with all that muscle what a man does.

The story of tattoos runs from the Maori tradition to today's studios, and loose shirts, cargo pants and sneakers have moved from men's wardrobes to women's. The writer recalls that in the Second World War the image of women working in factories became a symbol of strength, and that punk's rebellion is sold in shops today. The gist of her words is that even rebellion now has a brand and a sale season.
On social media she sees a strange democracy, where anyone can show themselves, but the currency of likes weighs heavy. The same carefree girl checks her phone every ten minutes.
Her conclusion is that this is not some new mould. She can wear a sari, bindi and bangles, and blush along with a tattoo. The real question is for the one watching: what answer was he waiting for?
nazar: The essay's strength is that even as it celebrates freedom, it puts a finger on the market's cunning. The range of a woman's choices has grown, but so has the reach of the companies that sell them to her and the algorithms that count likes.
sawal: Has the market packaged even women's rebellion?
ref: Rosie the Riveter
The iconic image of women working in American factories during the Second World War, which later became a symbol of women's strength.
Athleisure
A blend of sportswear and everyday wear: clothes that can be worn from the gym to the office and the market.

h: Four hundred and fifty stories at literature's labour chowk
dek: Anjali Deshpande and Kinshuk Gupta describe what came in to a story contest on workers, and how well Hindi fiction knows the worker.
body: The two co-editors of the web magazine 'Deemak' started a contest for stories about the working class. Their argument is that Hindi literature has written plenty about farmers, Dalits and women, and lately about queer people, Adivasis and religious intolerance too, but industrial and unorganised workers, trade unions and the changing world of labour have been almost left out, even though the number of workers and their struggles have grown.

About two and a half months were given and the last date was 30 October. The organisers expected few entries, but according to the writers, about 450 stories were in the inbox within two days. The memoir notes with light humour that although the poster asked for PDFs, people kept pasting stories into emails or sending drive links that would not open.

Most stories were about construction workers, the biggest sector of unorganised labour after farming, visible from every middle-class window. Plots such as a contractor holding back wages, medicine for a sick elder and school fees came up again and again, and in many stories children wake their parents up by explaining the sums to them. The writers ask whether such tidy solutions match reality. Some stories seemed written with the help of the internet and AI, with information but no lived experience.

Some entries opened up the very definition of labour, such as a story that saw urban sex work as labour. The stories with details of factory machines, production and the division of labour felt the strongest, and the writers felt these strengthen Dalit writers' claim that their work has a different aesthetic.
The organisers want to make it an annual event, with clear rules, but keeping room for unexpected readings.
nazar: Gig workers, contract labourers and construction sites are the real ground for stories in today's India, yet the Hindi short story is still often stuck in the village or the drawing room. Such efforts matter, provided the stories go beyond a ready recipe of pity and also show the structure of labour.
sawal: How long will the Hindi story avoid looking inside the factory?
ref: Labour chowk
City crossroads where daily-wage workers stand in the morning waiting for work and contractors pick them.
Unorganised sector
Work with no written contract, fixed wages or social security. Most of India's workers are in it.
photo_note: Blacksmith at the furnace, Patna Kalam

h: The last page of 'Invisible Cities' in Hindi
dek: The nineteenth instalment of Suman Shekhar's Hindi translation of Italo Calvino's 'Invisible Cities' on Sammukh has reached the book's final chapter.
body: In Italian writer Italo Calvino's book 'Invisible Cities', the Venetian traveller Marco Polo tells the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan about cities that perhaps exist nowhere. Young fiction writer Suman Shekhar is translating it into Hindi in instalments on Sammukh, and the nineteenth instalment covers the book's last chapter, the ninth part. We are not reproducing the translated text here, only introducing it.

The instalment is preceded by an editorial preface which says that every city carries its past: under floods, disasters and new construction, old layers survive. Many cities are known by stories tied to a house, a lane or a writer, and the same city is a homecoming for one person and a final farewell for another.

In this part the Khan has a huge atlas, with maps of every city, river and coast in his empire and beyond. Polo can give him no new information, so he talks about the listener: a listener remembers what he wanted to hear. Turning the pages, Polo recognises cities from Troy, Jericho and Carthage to Samarkand, Paris and Lhasa, and also imagines cities not yet built.
The chapter ends on the atlas's last pages, which hold unbuilt cities, ruined cities and webs of lines with no beginning or end. To read the translation, go to the instalment on Sammukh.
nazar: A young writer patiently bringing a difficult book of world literature into Hindi over nineteen instalments is the kind of work big publishers often do not do. At a time when cities are losing their layers to bulldozers and 'beautification', Calvino reminds us that cities are made more of memories than of bricks.
sawal: Which layer of your city is not recorded on the map?
ref: Italo Calvino (1923-1985)
Italian fiction writer whose 'Invisible Cities' (1972) describes imagined cities through conversations between Kublai Khan and Marco Polo.
Marco Polo
A thirteenth-century merchant-traveller from Venice who spent years at Kublai Khan's court and had an account of his travels written down.
